title: How I'm Making My Africa Unit More Knowledge Rich
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: This article by a primary teacher describes a curriculum redesign project aimed at making a geography unit on Africa genuinely knowledge-rich rather than merely fact-dense. Drawing heavily on the ideas in Developing Curriculum for Deep Thinking: The Knowledge Revival, the author distinguishes a knowledge-rich curriculum from a content-coverage curriculum: the former builds coherent, sequenced, revisited knowledge that forms interconnected mental models, while the latter presents isolated facts that fail to accumulate into durable schema. The author identifies three core principles — content richness, coherence, and clarity — and explains how her existing manufacturer-supplied unit violates all three through disconnected chapters and isolated topics. The redesign project focuses on selecting disciplinary knowledge deliberately, sequencing it logically, building recurring concepts, and ensuring vocabulary accumulates across the unit. The piece is a practical reflection on what it actually means to take cognitive science and curriculum research seriously at the classroom level.
points: A knowledge-rich curriculum is not about covering more content but about selecting knowledge deliberately, sequencing it logically, and revisiting it repeatedly so that students build increasingly connected mental models rather than collections of isolated facts.

The three core principles of a knowledge-rich curriculum — content richness, coherence, and clarity — are deeply interdependent: knowledge builds schema, schema supports thinking, and coherent integrated curriculum is what allows rich schema to develop over time.

Most commercially produced curriculum units violate knowledge-richness principles by presenting disconnected chapters and isolated facts, which means students are unlikely to build the durable, interconnected knowledge that enables critical and creative thinking.

The redesign process requires rethinking what knowledge to include, what to exclude, how to sequence it for maximum schema-building, and which vocabulary and concepts need to recur across the unit to accumulate meaningfully.

The kind of domain-specific knowledge that experts possess and that enables deep thinking cannot be built through a race to cover content — it develops only through curricula designed for coherence, depth, and logical progression.
quotes: A knowledge-rich curriculum is not a collection of facts. It is not a race to cover more content. It is not about teaching students more 'stuff.' And it is not the false choice between knowledge and thinking that often appears in education discussions.

A knowledge-rich curriculum is coherent. Knowledge and vocabulary is carefully selected, deliberately sequenced, and repeatedly revisited so students build increasingly connected mental models over time. New learning is attached to prior learning.

The more I study cognitive science and knowledge-rich curriculum research, the more I realize how connected these ideas are. Knowledge builds schema. Schema support thinking. And coherent integrated curriculum is what allows rich schema to develop over time.

As I take stock of my curriculum materials, it's obvious the unit as planned by the manufacturer is nothing more than a collection of disconnected facts and isolated chapters. That means students are not likely to be building durable, interconnected knowledge.

I started redesigning the unit around the core principles described in Developing Curriculum for Deep Thinking: The Knowledge Revival: coherence, disciplinary knowledge, schema building, logical sequencing, recurring concepts, knowledge that accumulates over time.

In other words, developing more meaningful, coherent, and interconnected knowledge in my students long-term memory. The kind of domain-specific knowledge experts possess and necessary for critical and creative thinking.
